q: Running mypy on a codebase with no annotations reports
options: Almost nothing, because an unannotated function is invisible to it
why: Which is why the file looks clean while being entirely unchecked.

options: An unannotated function from a blind spot into an error
An unannotated variable into an error
why: It is what makes "mypy passes" a statement about the whole file rather than the annotated half.

options: A function annotated `-> int` that returns something the checker only knows as `Any`
why: The most common way types quietly stop meaning anything, usually at the edge of an untyped library.

options: A guard, because one member of the union does not have that attribute
why: In practice the member without it is `None`.

options: Where the guarantees end, at the boundary with untyped code
Missing annotations on your own code
why: Which is why they are the errors people silence first and should not.

options: Silences every error on that line, including the one that appears there next year
Is equivalent to naming the code
why: Always name the code. `warn_unused_ignores` then tells you when it can go.

options: Returns its argument unchanged; nothing is converted and nothing is checked
Raises if the type is wrong
why: Honest about being an assertion, which is why it beats an ignore and loses to `isinstance`.

q: The best of the three escape hatches, when you can afford it, is
options: `assert isinstance(x, Foo)`, because it narrows and is genuinely checked
why: It cannot silently become wrong, which the other two can.

options: Makes mypy print what it believes `x` to be; it is not a real function and will fail at run time
Prints the type at run time
why: A question you ask the checker and then delete.

q: When a file reports several errors, read
options: The last one first, because an early mistake often cascades
Only the ones in your own code
why: Fixing the first frequently removes the rest.

q: The way to bring a checker to a large untyped codebase is
options: Defaults everywhere, then tighten module by module with overrides
Turn on strict and work through the list
Annotate everything first, then run it
why: Choose modules where a mistake is expensive, not the ones that look easy.

q: A third-party library with no types is handled by
options: Installing its stubs if they exist, and `ignore_missing_imports` for that module if not
why: One override in the config, rather than a comment in every file that imports it.

options: Overlap almost not at all; ruff does not check types
Are the same tool under different names
Different inference in places, so a codebase can pass one and not the other
why: Pick one for CI and let the other be an editor convenience.

why: A type expression that needs three lines is telling you something about the function, not the types.
